paragraphs.heading: A weighted average
paragraphs.text: The expected value of a random variable generalizes the weighted average. It also goes by the names expectation, mean or first moment. When the variable takes only finitely many values, it is exactly that average, with each value weighted by its probability. More generally it is defined as a Lebesgue integral of the variable with respect to the underlying probability measure. It is usually written E(X), E[X] or EX.

paragraphs.heading: The long run
paragraphs.text: When it is finite, the expected value can be read as the long-run average you would get from repeating the same random experiment independently. The law of large numbers is what turns that reading into a precise statement.

paragraphs.heading: The basic formula
paragraphs.text: Suppose X has a finite list of possible outcomes x₁,..., xₖ, with probabilities p₁,..., pₖ. Then E [X] = x₁p₁ + x₂p₂ + ⋯ + xₖpₖ. Because the probabilities must add up to 1, it is natural to read this as a weighted average of the outcomes.

paragraphs.heading: Born from a game
paragraphs.text: The idea grew in the mid-17th century out of the problem of points: how to split the stakes fairly when two players must stop a game early. In 1654 the Chevalier de Méré brought the problem to Blaise Pascal, who took it up in letters with Pierre de Fermat. Working independently, they reached identical results by different calculations, resting on one principle. A future gain should be valued in direct proportion to the chance of getting it. They did not publish, and told only a small circle of friends in Paris.

paragraphs.heading: Into print
paragraphs.text: Christiaan Huygens published a treatise on probability, "De ratiociniis in ludo aleæ", in 1657, soon after visiting Paris. It solved the problem of points on the same principle and added rules for harder cases, such as games with three or more players. The book can be seen as the first successful attempt to lay the foundations of probability theory. Later, in the mid-1800s, Pafnuty Chebyshev was the first person to think in a systematic way about the expectations of random variables.

paragraphs.heading: Many settings, one idea
paragraphs.text: The original definition handles finitely many outcomes, such as the flip of a coin. Infinite series stretch it to countably many outcomes, and it is also widely used for variables governed by continuous probability density functions. Measure theory and Lebesgue integration join all these cases as special cases of one general definition. It even extends to random vectors and random matrices, taken one component at a time.
